title: Character Classes & Quantifiers 🧮
description: Define sets of characters and control repetitions with *, +, ?, and {n,m}.

slides.title: Character Classes `[ ]` 🧱
slides.content:
## Match One of Many

Square brackets define a **character class** – a set of characters to match a single position.

- `[aeiou]` – any vowel.
- `[0-9]` – any digit (range).
- `[a-zA-Z]` – any letter.
- `[^abc]` – any character **NOT** a, b, or c (negated class).

Inside a class, most metacharacters lose their special meaning (except `^`, `-`, `]`).

slides.title: Vowel Finder
slides.content: List lines that contain at least one vowel:

quizData.question: What does `[^0-9]` match?

options.text: Any character that is NOT a digit

quizData.explanation: `^` at the start of a character class negates it.

slides.title: Predefined Character Classes 📋
slides.content:
## Shorthands

Many regex flavors support shortcuts:
- `\d` – digit `[0-9]`
- `\D` – non‑digit
- `\w` – word character `[a-zA-Z0-9_]`
- `\W` – non‑word
- `\s` – whitespace (space, tab, newline)
- `\S` – non‑whitespace

Note: `grep` doesn't support `\d` etc. unless you use `grep -P` (Perl‑compatible). Stick to `[0-9]` for portability.

slides.title: Simulating \d
slides.content: Match lines with digits using character class:

quizData.question: `grep -E '\d'` correctly matches digits.
quizData.explanation: Standard ERE doesn't support `\d`; you need `grep -P` or `[0-9]`.

slides.title: Quantifiers: *, +, ? 🔁
slides.content:
## How Many Times?

- `*` – zero or more of the preceding.
- `+` – one or more.
- `?` – zero or one (optional).

Examples:
- `ab*c` matches "ac", "abc", "abbc", etc.
- `ab+c` matches "abc", "abbc" but NOT "ac".
- `colou?r` matches both "color" and "colour".

quizData.question: Which regex matches an optional 's'?
quizData.explanation: `s?` makes the preceding character 's' optional, matching 'file' and 'files'.

slides.title: Fixed Repetition with `{n,m}` 🎯
slides.content:
## Precise Control

- `{n}` – exactly n times.
- `{n,}` – at least n times.
- `{n,m}` – between n and m times.

Examples:
- `[0-9]{3}` matches exactly three digits.
- `a{2,4}` matches "aa", "aaa", or "aaaa".

slides.title: Find Phone Numbers (simplified)
slides.content:
Match pattern 3 digits, dash, 4 digits:
```bash
echo 'Call 555-1234 now' | grep -E '[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}'
```

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Be careful: `.*` is greedy – it matches as much as possible. To match minimally, use `.*?` (not supported in ERE; need Perl regex `-P`).
